sections.description: Criminal Law Theory: Criminal Codes and Political Divisions Course Description: Blue Code, Red Code – Is a State’s Political Orientation Reflected in Its Criminal Law? The U.S. appears to be increasingly politically divided between “blue states” and “red states.” And the extent of the political division appears to be increasing. In 39 states, one party holds the governorship and both houses of the legislature. And such one-party rule has been increasing in recent years. This increasing partisan divide has even led some to suggest that the country should split along its blue-red divide, making it easier for blue states and red states to follow their separate paths. It would seem natural that the blue-red political divide would be reflected in significant differences between blue state and red state criminal codes. Indeed, some of the main hot button blue-red disputes concern criminal law: decriminalization of minor property crimes, the length of maximum sentences, the use of mandatory minimum sentences, the right to “stand your ground” when using deadly force against an aggressor, sentencing of drug offenses, recognition of a broad insanity defense, setting criminal law rules to maximize general deterrence and incapacitation of the dangerous rather than desert (blameworthiness proportionality), criminalizing abortion, and penalties for domestic violence, to name some of the more obvious issues. But even beyond these points of public political dispute, one might logically assume that the difference between blue state and red state values and perspectives would produce noticeable differences in all aspects of a state’s criminal law, whether an issue has become a major point of public debate or not. Is this assumption of blue code-red code differences borne out by the facts? Are blue codes and red codes systematically different? And, if so, what are those systematic differences and are they consistent with the publicly portrayed differences in values and perspectives of blue states and red states? The seminar will be a joint investigative project to undertake this inquiry. Each seminar meeting will focus on a different aspect of the state criminal codes and in preparation for each meeting students will study the relevant portion of one or more codes and report their findings to the group. Our focus will be on the 6 largest blue states (states in which Democrats control the governorship and both houses of the legislature) – California, New York, Illinois, Michigan, New Jersey, and Washington – and on the 6 largest red states – Texas, Florida, Ohio, Georgia, Tennessee, and Missouri. Our interest will be not only in mapping any blue-red differences but also in attempting to explain why differences exist (or do not exist). The seminar will also include readings on and discussions about the criminal law legislation and codification process. After the seminar, the project will be written up and published as a law review article and any student who chooses to continue with the publication project until it is complete (which can be done for course credit) will be a co-author on the article. Non-law students with strong academic records may register for the seminar with the prior permission of the instructor. For questions or additional information, contact Professor Robinson, phr@law.upenn.edu.
